title: Security Awareness Training
summary: Security awareness training is a planned programme that changes what employees do when they meet a phishing email, a strange login prompt or a request to move money. It is not a single annual slide deck. Mature programmes combine short induction content, regular short refreshers, realistic simulated phishing that is followed by coaching rather than punishment, role-specific modules for finance, engineering and executives, and a clear reporting path so that a person who spots something knows who to tell. The mechanism is behavioural: repeated, timely, low-friction prompts build a habit of pausing and verifying through a second channel. In a real environment the programme shows up in onboarding records, in the volume and speed of user-reported phishing, and in the outcome of exercises such as a payment-redirection test. The usual mistake is measuring completion rather than behaviour, which produces a workforce that can pass a quiz while still clicking a link, and punishing reporters, which drives the very reports you need into silence.

exercises.title: Security Awareness Training - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Security Awareness Training - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Security Awareness Training - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Security Awareness Training - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.

beginner.definition: Security awareness training teaches people how to spot and report common attacks at work. It uses short lessons, examples and practice messages. The goal is a habit, not a test score.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most attacks start with a message that a person opens. Technology alone cannot stop every one of them. Trained staff notice odd requests and ask a colleague before they act. They also report problems early, which gives the security team time to limit the damage.
howItWorks: New staff receive a short lesson on passwords, messages and reporting during induction.
Everyone gets regular and brief refreshers, instead of one long yearly session.
The team sends practice phishing messages and carefully watches who reports them.
People who click on a link receive a short coaching note, not a punishment.
Finance and engineering staff get extra lessons that match their daily risks.
Reported messages feed the security team, which removes similar ones from all inboxes.
beginner.example: Picture a shared kitchen in a large office. A poster on the wall tells everyone to check the gas before leaving. Nobody reads it after the first week. What actually works is a short reminder each Friday and a visible checklist by the door. A manager who thanks the person who speaks up helps even more. Security awareness training follows the same pattern. A yearly lecture fades quickly. Small repeated prompts and praise for reporting build a habit instead. When someone reports a strange email, they are the person who smelled gas. The team can then act before anyone is hurt.
takeaways: Measure whether people report suspicious messages, not whether they finished a course.
Thank people who report mistakes, because fear hides incidents.
Keep lessons short and repeat them often so the habit stays alive.

objectives: Explain the purpose of security awareness training in plain language.
Describe why a short repeated programme works better than one yearly session.
Design a simulated phishing exercise that coaches rather than punishes.
Identify role-specific training needs for finance, engineering and leadership staff.
Choose a behaviour measure that shows whether the programme is working.
